title: 10 Database Concepts You Can't Skip in System Design Interviews
summary: A ten-concept listicle covering the database fundamentals that come up in system design interviews: indexing, replication, sharding, partitioning, transactions, ACID, isolation levels, MVCC, locking and connection pooling. Each concept gets what it is, why it exists, a worked example, trade-offs and the interview takeaway.

chapters.title: 10 Database Concepts You Can't Skip
points: Cover title: 10 Database Concepts You Can't Skip in System Design Interviews
Ordered foundational to advanced: Indexing, Partitioning, Replication, Sharding, Transactions, ACID, Isolation Levels, MVCC, Locking, Connection Pooling
Each concept: what it is, why it exists, used for, a worked example, benefits, things to consider, interview takeaway
Swipe to build a vocabulary for any 'design a data layer' question

chapters.title: Indexing
points: What it is: a separate sorted structure (usually a B-tree) that maps column values to row locations so lookups skip a full table scan
Why it exists: a scan of 10M rows is O(n); a B-tree lookup is O(log n), about 3-4 page reads
Used for: WHERE filters, JOIN keys, ORDER BY, unique constraints
Worked example: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42 on 10M rows takes ~800 ms as a seq scan; after CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user ON orders(user_id) it takes ~1 ms (Index Scan in EXPLAIN)
Composite index (user_id, created_at) serves WHERE user_id=42 ORDER BY created_at, but not a filter on created_at alone (leftmost-prefix rule)
Benefit: orders-of-magnitude faster reads; covering indexes answer a query without touching the table
Benefit: unique indexes enforce constraints cheaply
Consider: every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must also update each index, so writes slow down and storage grows
Consider: low-cardinality columns (boolean, status) rarely benefit; wrapping the column in a function (LOWER(email)) skips the index
Interview takeaway: index for your read patterns, name the write-cost trade-off, and check with EXPLAIN

chapters.title: Partitioning
points: What it is: splitting one large table into smaller physical pieces (partitions) inside a single database server
Why it exists: huge tables make scans, index maintenance and deletes slow; smaller pieces are easier to manage
Used for: time-series data, logs, archival, fast bulk deletes of old data

Worked example: events table PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at) with monthly partitions; query for 2026-09 scans only events_2026_09 (partition pruning), and DROP TABLE events_2026_01 removes a month instantly instead of a slow DELETE
Strategies: range (dates), list (region = 'EU'), hash (user_id mod 8) for even spread
Benefit: partition pruning cuts scanned data; old data dropped in O(1)
Benefit: smaller per-partition indexes fit in memory
Consider: queries without the partition key scan every partition
Consider: the partition key must be part of primary and unique keys; too many partitions slow planning
Interview takeaway: partitioning is within one node for manageability; it is not the same as sharding across nodes

chapters.title: Replication
points: What it is: keeping copies of the same data on multiple servers, with a primary applying writes and replicas receiving them
Why it exists: availability if a node dies, read scaling, and geographic locality
Used for: failover, read-heavy workloads, analytics replicas, cross-region reads

Worked example: app writes to primary; replicas A and B stream the WAL. A user posts a comment, reads from replica A 200 ms later, and the comment is missing (replication lag), fixed by read-your-writes: route that user's reads to the primary for a few seconds
Synchronous replication waits for replica ack (no data loss, higher write latency); asynchronous returns immediately (fast, can lose recent writes on failover)
Topologies: single-leader (most common), multi-leader (needs conflict resolution), leaderless (quorum R + W > N)
Benefit: high availability through automatic failover
Benefit: read throughput scales by adding replicas
Consider: replication lag causes stale reads; failover can lose async writes or cause split-brain
Consider: replicas scale reads only, not writes
Interview takeaway: say single-leader with async replicas, then name lag and failover as the trade-offs

chapters.title: Sharding
points: What it is: horizontally splitting data across multiple independent database nodes, each holding a subset of rows (a shard)
Why it exists: one machine eventually hits limits on storage, write throughput and memory; replication does not scale writes
Used for: write-heavy, multi-terabyte datasets such as users, messages and orders at scale
Worked example: 4 shards, shard = hash(user_id) % 4; user_id 1001 maps to shard 1 and user_id 1002 to shard 2, so each shard takes about 25% of the writes
Strategies: hash (even load), range (efficient range scans, hotspot risk), directory/lookup table (flexible, extra hop)
Consistent hashing lets you add a node and move only about 1/N of keys instead of re-mapping all
Benefit: scales writes and storage nearly linearly
Benefit: failures and load are isolated to one shard
Consider: cross-shard joins and transactions are expensive or unsupported
Consider: a bad shard key creates hotspots (a celebrity user_id) and resharding is painful
Interview takeaway: shard last; pick a key with high cardinality that matches your dominant query, and note replication runs inside each shard

chapters.title: Transactions
points: What it is: a group of operations executed as one unit of work that either all commit or all roll back
Why it exists: multi-step changes can fail midway (crash, constraint error) and leave data half-updated
Used for: money transfers, order placement with stock decrement, any multi-row invariant

Worked example: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2; COMMIT; if the second UPDATE fails, ROLLBACK restores account 1 to its original balance
Lifecycle: BEGIN, statements, then COMMIT or ROLLBACK; SAVEPOINT allows partial rollback
Benefit: no partial writes, so the invariant 'total money is unchanged' always holds
Benefit: simpler application code since the database handles cleanup
Consider: long transactions hold locks and bloat undo or dead rows
Consider: transactions across shards or services need 2PC or sagas
Interview takeaway: keep transactions short, and say what you do when they span services (saga)

chapters.title: ACID
points: What it is: four guarantees of a reliable transaction: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
Why it exists: defines what 'correct' means when failures and concurrency happen
Used for: judging whether a store is safe for payments, inventory and bookings
Atomicity: all or nothing, implemented with an undo log or rollback
Consistency: the transaction moves data between valid states, enforced by constraints such as CHECK (balance >= 0) and foreign keys
Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work; its strength is tunable
Durability: once COMMIT returns, data survives a crash because the write-ahead log (WAL) is fsynced to disk before ack
Worked example: transfer of 100 from A (balance 50) violates CHECK (balance >= 0), so the whole transaction aborts and neither account changes (A + C)
Benefit: predictable correctness under crashes and concurrency
Consider: ACID costs latency and throughput; many NoSQL stores relax it for BASE (eventual consistency)
Consider: the C in ACID is app-defined invariants, not the C in CAP theorem
Interview takeaway: be able to explain each letter with one mechanism (undo log, constraints, isolation level, WAL)

chapters.title: Isolation Levels
points: What it is: a setting that controls how much concurrent transactions can see of each other's uncommitted or newly committed changes
Why it exists: full isolation is expensive, so databases let you trade correctness for throughput
Used for: tuning per-workload safety, for example reports versus payments
Anomalies: dirty read (see uncommitted data), non-repeatable read (same row changes between two reads), phantom read (new rows match a repeated query), write skew
Read Uncommitted allows dirty reads; Read Committed (Postgres default) blocks dirty reads; Repeatable Read blocks non-repeatable reads; Serializable behaves as if transactions ran one at a time
Worked example: T1 reads balance 100; T2 updates it to 50 and commits; T1 reads again. At Read Committed T1 sees 50 (non-repeatable read); at Repeatable Read T1 still sees 100
Write skew example: two on-call doctors both check 'at least 2 on call' and both go off call; only Serializable prevents it
Benefit: lower levels give higher concurrency and fewer blocks or retries
Consider: Serializable may abort transactions, so the app must retry on serialization failure
Consider: defaults differ (MySQL InnoDB Repeatable Read, Postgres Read Committed) and Postgres Repeatable Read is snapshot isolation
Interview takeaway: default to Read Committed, name the anomaly you are guarding against, and escalate only where needed

chapters.title: MVCC
points: What it is: Multi-Version Concurrency Control keeps several versions of a row so readers see a consistent snapshot without blocking writers
Why it exists: plain read/write locks make readers wait for writers, hurting throughput
Used for: implementing snapshot isolation in Postgres, MySQL InnoDB and Oracle

Worked example in Postgres: each row has xmin and xmax transaction ids; T100 updates a row, creating a new version with xmin=100 and marking the old one xmax=100; T99, whose snapshot predates 100, still reads the old version
Readers never block writers and writers never block readers; writers on the same row still conflict
Postgres stores old versions in the table and VACUUM reclaims dead tuples; InnoDB keeps old versions in undo logs
Benefit: high read concurrency with consistent snapshots
Benefit: long read-only queries do not lock anyone
Consider: bloat from dead rows if VACUUM lags, and long-running transactions pin old versions
Consider: write-write conflicts still need locks or abort on first-updater-wins
Interview takeaway: say 'readers don't block writers' and mention vacuum or undo cleanup as the cost

chapters.title: Locking
points: What it is: a mechanism that makes a transaction hold exclusive or shared claim on rows or tables so others wait
Why it exists: concurrent writers to the same data would otherwise cause lost updates
Used for: protecting hot rows such as inventory counts, seat bookings and balances
Types: shared (read) locks, exclusive (write) locks, row-level versus table-level
Pessimistic locking: SELECT stock FROM items WHERE id=7 FOR UPDATE blocks other writers until commit
Optimistic locking: UPDATE items SET stock=stock-1, version=version+1 WHERE id=7 AND version=12; if 0 rows updated, retry
Worked example: two buyers purchase the last ticket; without a lock both read stock=1 and both succeed (lost update), with FOR UPDATE the second waits and then sees stock=0
Deadlock: T1 locks row A then wants B while T2 locks B then wants A; the DB detects and aborts one, so lock rows in a consistent order
Benefit: guarantees correctness on contended rows
Consider: lock contention and deadlocks reduce throughput; use pessimistic for high contention and optimistic for low contention
Interview takeaway: choose pessimistic versus optimistic by contention level and mention retries and lock ordering

chapters.title: Connection Pooling
points: What it is: a cache of open database connections that application requests borrow and return instead of opening a new one each time
Why it exists: opening a connection costs a TCP and TLS handshake plus authentication and, in Postgres, a whole backend process (several MB of RAM)
Used for: every web service talking to a database; pgbouncer, HikariCP, RDS Proxy
Worked example: 50 app instances each with 20 connections is 1000 connections, but Postgres max_connections is 100; put PgBouncer in transaction mode so 1000 clients share 50 server connections
Pool sizing rule of thumb: connections ≈ (core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count; for an 8-core DB about 17 is a good start
Modes: session, transaction and statement pooling; transaction mode breaks session features such as prepared statements and SET
Benefit: removes about 20-50 ms of connect latency per request
Benefit: caps load so the database is not overwhelmed
Consider: a pool that is too large causes contention, too small causes request queueing and timeouts
Consider: leaked connections (not returned) exhaust the pool, so always release in finally blocks
Interview takeaway: size the pool to the database's capacity, not to the number of clients, and put a proxy in front when you scale app instances

chapters.title: Database Concepts Cheatsheet
points: Indexing: B-tree, O(log n) reads, slower writes; leftmost-prefix rule
Partitioning: split a table inside one node; pruning by partition key
Replication: copies for availability and read scale; watch lag
Sharding: split data across nodes for write scale; shard key choice is critical
Transactions: all-or-nothing units; keep them short
ACID: atomicity (undo), consistency (constraints), isolation, durability (WAL)
Isolation levels: Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable; know the anomalies
MVCC: row versions, readers do not block writers; vacuum cost
Locking: pessimistic FOR UPDATE versus optimistic version column; avoid deadlocks via ordering
Connection pooling: size to the DB, use PgBouncer or HikariCP
